review.material: Complete 48-page PDF text layer read; selected diagrams on PDF pp.5–7, 21–22, 30–32 and 46 visually inspected.
review.limitations: This is a selection of visual demonstrations, not a full audit of every artwork or diagram. Philosophical claims and teaching examples are not a controlled user study or proof that an implementation exceeds Turing computation. PDF remains link-only because it contains excluded third-party images.

evidence.description: Embedding, alternative parts and figure–ground readings
Schemas, changing decompositions and triangle examples

sections.title: What the slides demonstrate
sections.text: A visual introduction to calculation that can discover new parts in a drawing rather than preserve one fixed inventory of pieces.

sections.title: Central premise
sections.text: A rule can match an embedded shape even when that shape differs from the objects originally drawn. Fusion permits later rules to divide the result differently.

sections.title: How the demonstration works
sections.text: Nested squares, figure–ground reversals and triangle arrangements alternate with rule schemas. The diagrams contrast the geometry visible now with a retrospective decomposition tree.

sections.title: The rule-application mechanism
sections.text: For A→B in host C, find t(A)≤C, then calculate (C−t(A))+t(B). The same transformation t places both sides; after fusion, the next match can select different parts.

sections.title: How to interpret the outcome
sections.text: These are explanatory examples and philosophical arguments. The slides qualify their discussion of symbolic and visual computation; they do not establish a benchmark showing that a particular computer program has unlimited visual insight.

sections.title: A practical reading task
sections.text: Trace a part that crosses earlier drawing boundaries, apply one rule, then redraw a different decomposition of the result. Compare the geometry with its description tree.
